title: DINGDAR Launches Its International Website
excerpt: Our new English website is now live. Buyers of crusher wear parts, bucket teeth and custom castings can send drawings, part numbers or samples directly for a technical review and quotation.
coverAlt: Foundry worker pouring molten metal into molds
body: Henan Dingdar Machinery Equipment Manufacture Co., Ltd. has launched its international website at dingdar.com to make it easier for overseas buyers to start a casting project. The site covers the full product range — jaw crusher wear parts, cone crusher wear parts, impact crusher blow bars, hammer heads, double roll crusher parts, bucket teeth and adapters, and custom castings produced to drawing or sample.

Every inquiry is reviewed as a technical requirement: geometry, material, casting process and inspection scope are confirmed before price and delivery are quoted. Buyers can start with a drawing, a 3D model, a part number, or simply a photo of the worn part.

Inquiries can be submitted through the contact form on the website, by email to hugo@dingdar.com, or via WhatsApp at +86 19337861987. The project team aims to reply with technical feedback within 12–24 hours.

The site also explains our four in-house casting routes — green sand, shell moulding, lost foam and investment casting — and the material families used across wear parts and custom components, based on over 40 years of casting experience since 1986.

title: How to Choose Jaw Plate Material: Mn13 and Mn18
excerpt: Jaw plates fail by impact, abrasion or both. A practical guide to high-manganese steel grades, when to move to alloy options, and what to send the foundry so the material choice is made on facts.
coverAlt: Two workers managing molten metal in an industrial furnace
body: Jaw plate material is not a one-size choice. A plate that lasts well in one quarry can fail early in another, usually because the feed conditions — rock hardness, size, moisture and the crusher setup — change the failure mode. Understanding which mode is wearing your plates is the first step to choosing the right material; the second is knowing what each grade family can and cannot do.

Read the wear pattern before looking at a grade table. The failure mode tells you which property the part actually needs:
Failure modeWhat the part needsUsual direction
Smooth, polished wear face, little deformationHigher initial hardnessMove away from Hadfield manganese toward alloy or composite grades
Gouging, metal flow, peened surfaceToughness under repeated impactStandard Mn13 duty, or Mn18 for heavier plates
Breakage through the plate bodyToughness plus section design reviewManganese, with the geometry and clamping checked — a harder grade makes it worse
Cracks starting at bolt holes or thin sectionsSection and preload review firstMaterial change alone will not fix this
One-sided or end-only wearFeed or setting correctionFix the machine condition before buying a different grade
That table is why the same part number is legitimately supplied in different grades to different pits.

For the great majority of primary and secondary jaw applications, high-manganese steel in the Mn13 and Mn18 families is the standard. Under repeated impact, the surface work-hardens: the top layer compresses into a much harder skin while the core stays tough, so the plate resists both impact and abrasion at the same time. Mn13 (about 13% manganese, typically matching an ASTM A128-grade equivalent) covers standard quarry feed; Mn18 with slightly higher manganese and refined treatment is specified where feed is harder or plates are larger and more likely to flex.

There are cases where manganese steel is not the best start. If the feed is mostly fines with little impact energy, a manganese plate may not work-harden properly and can wear smoothly; an alloy steel or a composite with higher initial hardness can last longer. If the feed contains very large, hard boulders, toughness matters more than hardness, and the balance shifts back toward manganese. This is why we ask about feed size, abrasiveness and the crusher model before quoting — the grade is selected against your working conditions, not a menu. The trade-off is always the same: hardness resists abrasion, toughness resists breakage, and the right answer depends on which of those is ending the plate life in your plant.

What you should send the foundry to get a reliable recommendation: the crusher model and closed-side setting, the typical feed size and rock type (for example granite, basalt, limestone, ore), the current plate life in hours or tonnage and the failure pattern — broken, peened, or smooth-worn. Two plates of the same part number often need different materials for different pits, and the review exists to catch that before production. We produce jaw plates in Mn13, Mn18 and variants, and review alloy options per application. Send the part number or drawing with your working conditions and the technical review will confirm the material, hardness and inspection scope before any quote is prepared. Browse the jaw crusher wear parts range for an overview of what we cast, read the Mn13 jaw plate guide for grade detail, or start the review with a part number or photo of the worn plate through the contact form.

metaDescription: How MOQ, tooling and lead time are confirmed for crusher wear parts, and what buyers should send for a faster technical quotation.
title: MOQ, Tooling and Lead Time for Crusher Wear Parts
excerpt: Why a foundry cannot quote MOQ and lead time without seeing the part — and the three questions that unlock a fast, reliable answer for crusher wear parts and custom castings.
coverAlt: Molten steel being handled in an industrial foundry
body: Inquiries that begin with "what is your MOQ?" usually get a frustrating answer from a foundry: it depends on the part. This is not a delay tactic. MOQ, tooling and lead time are all driven by the geometry of one specific casting, and quoting them before the part is known would simply be a guess. What a buyer can do is understand which variables drive the number, so the answer arrives in one round instead of five.

MOQ is driven by economics, not policy. A pattern or tooling set costs the same whether you cast one piece or a thousand, and that cost has to be spread across the order. A small, simple part that pours in one mould can be produced in low quantities at a fair price per piece; a large jaw plate that occupies a full mould and needs long cooling and heat-treatment time makes small runs expensive per piece. The variables that move the number are consistent:
VariableEffect on MOQ and unit cost
Pattern equipment (new or existing)Amortised across the order — a new pattern pushes the economic MOQ up; reusing an existing one pulls it down
Mould size and part weightHeavy parts consume mould capacity, so fewer pieces fit a shift
Material and heat treatmentManganese steel needs a controlled heat-treatment cycle; small heats are inefficient
Machining and inspection scopePer-piece operations that do not scale down — NDT or third-party inspection especially
Order frequencyA frame quantity spread over a year is priced differently from a single shipment

Lead time follows the same logic. Geometry decides the pattern or tooling route and how long that takes. Material and inspection scope decide the production steps — a manganese casting needs a long, controlled heat treatment after pouring, and NDT or third-party inspection adds days at the end. Quantity decides whether production can be phased. Once the part reference is known, we can separate "part of the time is the casting, part is the tooling" instead of giving one opaque figure. Some stages compress and some do not:
  • Can be compressed: pattern making (parallel to material procurement), machining slots, inspection booking, and shipping consolidation
  • Cannot be compressed without risking the part: cooling after pouring, the heat-treatment cycle, and any ageing or stress-relief step the grade requires
Squeezing the second group is how castings arrive early and fail early.

The three questions that unlock a fast answer are: (1) the part number, drawing, sample or machine model; (2) the material or hardness you need — or the application, so we can propose it; (3) the annual or per-order quantity and the delivery market. Add the incoterm and destination port if logistics is part of the decision, because freight and packing can dominate the landed cost of heavy castings. With those three, a foundry can confirm tooling, MOQ, lead time and the inspection scope in writing — usually within a week for a first quotation.

There are legitimate ways to lower the per-piece cost without waiting for volume: reuse or share existing pattern equipment where the same plate family covers several crusher models, combine several part numbers from one machine into a single order so packing and freight are shared, and split an annual requirement into scheduled releases. The practical takeaway for buyers: do not delay the inquiry until you have a full drawing. A part number or a photo of the worn part, plus quantity and destination, is enough to start the review. Everything else — exact dimensions, tolerances, marking and documents — gets confirmed during the review, before any commitment. Send those three items through the contact form, and read what a quotation needs if you want to prepare the full set.

metaDescription: Green sand casting advantages and disadvantages compared with investment casting, shell moulding and lost foam for wear parts, tolerance, finish and volume.
title: Green Sand Casting: Advantages and Disadvantages vs Investment
excerpt: Green sand handles large wear castings at competitive cost; investment casting delivers precision on small components. How foundries match the process to the part — and when both are the wrong answer.
coverAlt: Foundry worker managing a furnace in an industrial plant
body: Choosing a casting process is often presented as a quality ladder: investment is "better" than green sand. In practice the right route is the one that matches the part size, geometry, tolerances and volume — and a foundry that casts everything one way is probably pushing a single pattern through your requirement.

Green sand casting is the workhorse for medium and large castings. Sand is packed around the pattern, the mould is used once, and the process handles a very wide range of sizes and materials at competitive cost. Dimensional accuracy is standard, surface finish is standard, and tooling is relatively fast — which makes it the natural choice for large wear parts such as jaw plates and housings, and for anything heavy enough that precision casting would be impractical.

Investment casting starts with a wax pattern and a ceramic shell; it delivers the highest dimensional accuracy and surface finish in the family, and it suits smaller components with fine detail and tight tolerances. The trade-off is cost and cycle time per part, so it earns its place where the precision saves machining or where geometry cannot be produced any other way. Shell moulding and lost foam sit between the two — better finish than green sand for repeatable series, and near-net-shape capability that can remove machining steps from a part that would otherwise need it.

The differences that decide the route are worth putting side by side, because "better" is not one of the columns:
RouteTypical fitTrade-off
Green sandMedium to large wear parts, wide size range, cost-sensitive volumeStandard tolerance and finish; machining allowance usually needed
Shell mouldingRepeatable series needing better finish and sharper detail than green sandPattern and shell cost per mould; less economical for one-offs
Lost foamComplex geometry, fewer joints, near-net shapePattern per part, and the foam pattern is consumed each cycle
InvestmentSmall parts with fine detail and tight tolerancesHighest cost and cycle time per piece; size range is limited

The practical rule we apply in review: part size and order volume narrow the route first, then tolerance and finish requirements decide how far up the precision scale you need to go. A heavy crusher component cast to loose tolerances does not benefit from investment casting; a small valve component with fine detail would not be economical in green sand. Sometimes different components in one assembly correctly use different routes, planned together so material and inspection stay consistent. Because the process choice drives tooling, cost and lead time, we confirm the route during the technical review against the drawing and working conditions — then quote on that confirmed basis. Send the part number, drawing or sample through the contact form, and the review will tell you which route fits and why; the process selection guide compares the four routes in more detail.

title: How to Identify the Correct Jaw Plate for Your Crusher
excerpt: Ordering the wrong jaw plate costs downtime and money. A practical checklist for identifying the correct plate from part numbers, drawings, measurements and worn-part photos before you send a request.
coverAlt: High-manganese steel jaw plates for a jaw crusher
body: A jaw plate looks like a simple casting, but the differences between plates are easy to underestimate: crusher brand and model, chamber profile, tooth shape, bolt-hole pattern and revision level all change the part. An inquiry that starts with the correct identification usually saves two or three rounds of clarification — and avoids casting the wrong part at all. The points below are the ones that most often decide whether a plate is quoted correctly the first time.

Start with the part number and the machine. The fastest identifier is the part number cast or stamped on the plate, or the crusher model from the nameplate. Read the nameplate in full rather than copying the model from a purchase record, and note:
  • brand, series and exact model designation
  • feed opening and, where shown, the setting range
  • serial number and year of manufacture
  • any OEM or licence marking on the plate itself
If the part number is worn away, the machine model alone is usually enough for a foundry to narrow the plate family, because each crusher series has a defined set of jaw plates. The serial number matters when a manufacturer changed plate geometry mid-series without renaming the model.

Then confirm the geometry. Note the chamber type (standard, coarse or fine), the tooth profile (wave, straight or custom), the position and spacing of the bolt holes, the thickness, and whether the plate is the fixed or movable jaw — they are not interchangeable. A practical measurement set is: overall length and width, thickness at the thickest and thinnest point, tooth pitch, bolt-hole diameter and centre-to-centre distance, and the distance from the mounting face to the wear face. Take them with a tape and a calliper on the worn plate, and record the weight if the plate can be weighed. Weight is the single quickest cross-check: two plates with the same part number but noticeably different weight are not the same casting.

Photograph the worn plate properly, because the wear pattern carries diagnostic information that a description rarely captures. A set of photos — the wear face, the back face, the mounting face and the worn profile from the side — tells a foundry more than paragraphs. Read the pattern before sending it:
What you seeWhat it usually means
Smooth, polished wear face with little deformationLow impact energy — manganese may not be work-hardening; consider a harder starting grade
Deep gouging or metal flow at the feed endHigh impact from oversized feed; toughness matters more than hardness
Even wear across the whole faceBalanced chamber; a material change is unlikely to gain much life
Cracks starting at bolt holes or thin sectionsSection design, clamping or thermal stress — a material change alone will not fix it
Uneven wear, one side much deeperFeed segregation or a mis-set chamber; fix the cause before changing the plate
Correct identification is the precondition for this reading: a wear pattern only means something against the right part and the right operating conditions.

Send the part number, machine model, key measurements and photos together, and the technical review confirms the identity, material and hardness before any quotation. If you are unsure whether two plates are the same, say so in the message — the review exists to catch that before production, not after. If the plate is out of production or the OEM part number no longer exists, a drawing or a measured worn part is enough to reverse-engineer the geometry, and the review will state which dimensions have to be agreed before a pattern is made. Related reading: how to choose jaw plate material and Mn13 jaw plates in detail, or send the details through the contact form.

metaDescription: Five items to prepare for a crusher wear parts quotation: part reference, application, quantity, acceptance criteria and destination.
title: Information Needed for a Custom Crusher Wear Parts Quote
excerpt: A foundry can quote faster and more accurately when it has the right starting information. The five things to prepare before requesting a custom crusher wear parts quotation.
coverAlt: Worker operating machinery near molten metal and intense flames
body: The speed and accuracy of a casting quotation depend almost entirely on the starting information. With a complete set, a foundry can confirm tooling, material, MOQ, lead time and inspection scope in writing within a week; without it, the quote comes back full of assumptions or the review needs several rounds. Preparing the five items below removes most of that friction.

First, the part reference — the single most important item. A part number, drawing, 3D model or sample is what the foundry needs to identify geometry and start the review. If you have a drawing, send the revision that is actually current and say so; a drawing marked Rev. C and a purchase order written against Rev. B is a common and expensive mismatch. A neutral 3D format (STEP or IGES) removes ambiguity about radii, draft and fillet details that 2D views hide. If you have only a photo of the worn part, send it anyway: it is enough to begin, and the missing details get confirmed during the review.

Second, the application. The crusher model, typical feed size, rock type and whether the part runs in primary or secondary duty decide the material recommendation. Two identical part numbers running in different pits can need different grades, so the application is not optional detail — it is the basis of the material choice. Useful specifics: the feed opening and closed-side setting you run, the largest lump in the feed, and whether the plant works wet or dry. If wear life is the complaint behind the inquiry, say what the current part achieved and in what tonnage — that single number reframes the whole review.

Third, quantity and plan. Order volume, whether it is a first order or a repeat, and the delivery market determine tooling amortization, MOQ and lead time. Annual or frame quantities can be spread across the year rather than shipped at once, which usually lowers the per-piece cost. If several part numbers belong to the same machine or the same wear cycle, list them together: a combined order shares packing, freight and inspection booking, and often shares pattern equipment.

Fourth, acceptance and documentation. If your project requires a specific material standard, hardness range, NDT or third-party inspection, state it before the quotation: acceptance criteria are agreed in writing before production, and adding them afterwards costs time and money. Each item you supply changes a specific part of the quote, which is why a vague inquiry produces a quote with wide ranges:
InformationWhat it changes in the quote
Drawing revision and 3D modelPattern design, machining allowance, whether new tooling is needed at all
Material or gradeMelting practice, heat-treatment cycle, achievable hardness
Application and dutyThe grade recommendation itself — the item most often missing
Quantity and delivery scheduleTooling amortisation, MOQ, phasing of production
Inspection and documentsCost per piece and the days added at the end of the run

Fifth, contact details and destination country — small, but they let the foundry confirm logistics and documents in the same reply, including packing for sea freight, marking requirements and which certificate language is needed. Review the custom castings range, then send all five items through the contact form, by email to hugo@dingdar.com or on WhatsApp. The project team responds with technical feedback within 12–24 hours.

metaDescription: Which material, dimensional, hardness, visual and NDT records buyers should request for crusher wear parts before shipment.
title: Inspection Records to Request for Crusher Wear Parts
excerpt: Material certificates, dimensional reports, hardness records, NDT — which inspection evidence matters for crusher wear parts, and how to specify it so it ships with your order.
coverAlt: Quality inspection of cast parts at the DINGDAR foundry
body: Inspection records are what turn a quotation into a verifiable order. Buyers who specify the records they need before production receive evidence with the shipment; buyers who ask afterwards usually wait. For crusher wear parts, the meaningful records fall into a short list, and each one serves a different purpose — which is why asking for "all certificates" tends to produce paper rather than evidence.

Material certificates (heat or melt analysis) are the core record: they confirm the grade that was actually poured, against the standard agreed for the order — for manganese steel, for example, the chemistry of the Mn13 or Mn18 family per an ASTM, DIN or GB equivalent. Three checks make the certificate worth reading:
  • the heat number on the certificate matches the heat number marked on the casting
  • the chemistry is compared against the agreed standard, not against a generic "manganese steel" description
  • carbon equivalent is stated where the part will be welded in service
A certificate without a traceable heat number proves that some compliant steel was poured somewhere — not that this part was made from it.

Dimensional, hardness and visual records cover the delivered part itself, and each answers a different question. Dimensional reports confirm the part against the drawing: the critical dimensions, the bolt-hole positions and the tolerances. Hardness records show the delivered hardness range, which matters for wear parts where hardness is the accepted indicator of performance — read as-cast values against the agreed range, and treat surface hardness separately from core hardness where the grade work-hardens. Visual inspection records cover surface quality, marking and obvious defects. For most crusher wear parts this trio, plus the material certificate, is the working set:
RecordWhat it provesWhen it earns its cost
Material certificateThe grade poured and its chemistryAlways — it is the base record
Dimensional reportFit and interchangeabilityAlways for OEM replacement parts
Hardness recordThe delivered condition after heat treatmentAlways for wear parts
Visual / marking recordTraceability and surface acceptanceAlways, and cheap to add

NDT — ultrasonic, magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing — is specified where internal soundness matters most, such as structural castings or parts that will take heavy impact, and where a casting defect would cause a failure rather than faster wear. Third-party inspection by an agreed body can be added when your project or your customer requires independent verification, and is usually arranged against a named scope rather than as a general instruction. Each of these has a cost, so the scope should match the part, not be added uniformly: a blow bar and a 6-tonne frame do not need the same testing.

The way to get the right records is to specify them in the review: material standard, hardness range, dimensional checks, NDT or third-party inspection, and the documentation language. Records should be agreed with the order and travel with the shipment, because a certificate that arrives after the container has been released cannot stop a bad part from being installed. DINGDAR agrees the inspection and acceptance scope before production and ships the agreed records with the order — so the buyer's incoming inspection step is short and the evidence trail is complete. See the jaw crusher wear parts page for the dimensional points that are usually inspected, read what information a quote needs, or send your required inspection scope through the contact form.

title: What Factors Affect the Service Life of Crusher Wear Parts?
excerpt: The same part can last twice as long in one plant and fail early in another. The four groups of factors that determine crusher wear part life — and how to act on each.
coverAlt: Worker in protective gear welding metal in an industrial plant
body: Service life is the number buyers care about most, and the honest starting point is that the part is only half the story. The same jaw plate or blow bar can wear at very different rates between plants because of factors outside the casting itself. Understanding the four groups below explains most of the difference — and tells you which of them you can actually change.

Working conditions come first. Rock hardness and abrasiveness, feed size, moisture and clay content set the wear rate before anything else. Highly abrasive feed wears a plate quickly no matter the grade; wet, sticky feed changes the wear pattern entirely, packing in the chamber and loading the part differently. When life numbers are compared between plants, the feed conditions have to be part of the comparison — otherwise a grade that performs well in one quarry looks like a failure in another for reasons that have nothing to do with the steel.

Crusher settings come second. Closed-side setting, speed or eccentric throw, and the uniformity of the feed all change how the part is loaded. Too large a reduction ratio, an uneven feed or a plate running with the wrong setting accelerates wear and can produce failure patterns that look like a material fault but are actually a machine-setting fault. Segregated feed — fines down one side, coarse down the other — produces the classic one-sided wear profile, and no material change will correct it.

Material and heat treatment come third — the part of the equation the foundry controls. High-manganese steel work-hardens under impact, so it suits high-impact duty; where impact energy is low, an alloy or composite with higher initial hardness lasts longer. Matching the grade to the actual impact energy of the machine is what turns a good grade into the right grade. This is also why the same part number can legitimately be ordered in two different grades for two different plants.

Installation and operation come fourth. Bolt preload, seating and whether plates are turned or swapped according to wear all affect useful life; a plate that moves in its seat cracks early regardless of material. The practical way to improve life across orders is to record it consistently, so the next inquiry carries evidence instead of an impression:
RecordWhy it changes the next order
Tonnage or hours achieved per liner setTurns "it wore out fast" into a number the foundry can design against
Photos of the worn part, plus the wear profile from the sideSeparates impact wear from abrasion, and one-sided wear from uniform wear
Feed size and rock type during that periodExplains differences between two sites running the same part
Closed-side setting and any changes made mid-lifeRules out a machine-setting cause before changing material
Where and how it failed (crack, break, wear-through)Distinguishes a material problem from a design or installation problem
Send that history with the inquiry and the foundry can adjust material or design instead of guessing — which is how life gets extended rather than replaced. Compare the jaw crusher wear parts and blow bar ranges, or read how jaw plate material is chosen.

title: Cone Crusher Liners: Mantle, Concave & Bowl Liner Guide
excerpt: Cone crusher liners are the largest recurring wear cost in secondary and tertiary crushing circuits. A step-by-step guide to identifying the mantle, concave and bowl liner from part numbers, measurements and worn-part photos — and the material options that match your feed conditions.
coverAlt: Two workers managing molten metal in an industrial furnace
body: **Direct answer:** A cone crusher liner set is two castings: the mantle, the moving liner on the gyrating head, and the concave or bowl liner, the stationary ring on the frame. Brands do not agree on the stationary name — some use concave for the upper ring and bowl liner for a separate lower component, others use both names for the same casting — so a liner is identified by position, by chamber (coarse, medium or fine) and by crusher model, then confirmed with part number, key dimensions and photos of the worn part. High-manganese steel in the Mn13 and Mn18 families, the ASTM A128 grades, is the industry baseline; a high-chromium iron in roughly the Cr15–Cr26 range takes over where the feed is fine and wear is dominated by sliding abrasion rather than impact.

## Mantle, concave or bowl liner: what each name means

Terminology is where many inquiries go wrong before they even start. The moving liner is called the mantle on virtually every brand. The stationary ring is where names split: some manufacturers call it the concave, others the bowl liner, and a few use both names for different parts of the same assembly.

| Part | Position | Names in use | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mantle | Moving liner on the gyrating head | Mantle, universally | Crushes on the moving side and, with the stationary ring, forms the chamber |
| Concave | Stationary upper ring | Concave; bowl liner on some ranges | Crushes on the fixed side of the chamber |
| Bowl liner | Stationary lower ring, where it is a separate component | Bowl liner; also used loosely for the whole stationary ring | Closes the discharge end of the chamber |

In one well-known range the concave is the upper ring and the bowl liner is a separate lower component; in another brand the two terms describe the same casting. Quoting "the part on the left when you stand facing the feed" is surprisingly common in real inquiries. The reliable way to describe a liner is by position (moving or stationary), by chamber (coarse, medium or fine) and by the crusher model and feed opening — that combination removes almost all ambiguity.

## Why the same crusher can run different liners

A cone crusher crushes by compression. The mantle is mounted on the main shaft, which is carried in an eccentric that makes the head gyrate inside the fixed concave ring; the crushing chamber between the two surfaces narrows toward the discharge end, and rock is broken as it is squeezed between the moving and stationary liners.

Because the liner profile defines the shape of that chamber, the liner is doing two jobs at once: it protects the structural steel and it sets the reduction ratio, the throughput and the product shape. A coarse-profile liner opens the chamber for high throughput with a coarser product; a fine profile closes the chamber for better reduction and shape at lower capacity. The same crusher can therefore legitimately run different liners, and that is the first reason a machine model alone cannot identify a part.

## Four sources of evidence that identify a liner

The fastest identifier is still the part number, normally cast into the back of the liner or stamped on a tag. But a part number is only as trustworthy as the drawing behind it. In the aftermarket, liners are frequently repoured: a supplier takes an original pattern or scans a used liner, and the result can be close in outline yet different in wear-band thickness, bolt-hole spacing or chamber geometry. The same part number from two suppliers can produce different life and different product.

Identification should therefore combine four sources of evidence: the part number, the crusher brand and model from the nameplate, a set of key dimensions, and photographs of the worn liner. The dimension set that matters for a cone liner is short, and it is the check that catches a drifted pattern before production rather than after.

| Measurement | Where it is taken | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top inner diameter | Feed end of the liner | Chamber opening and profile drift |
| Bottom inner diameter | Discharge end | Reduction ratio and setting range |
| Overall height | Working face to mounting face | A worn part reproduced short |
| Wear-band thickness | Thickest section of the working face | A pattern cut from a worn liner coming out thin |
| Bolt pattern | Mounting face | Hole spacing that will not seat |

## Photographs: three shots that do most of the work

Photographs deserve a short method of their own. Three shots are usually enough: the wear face showing the profile, the back or mounting face, and a close view of the worn profile edge.

The value of the photos goes beyond identification. The shape of the wear tells the material reviewer how the liner was loaded — whether the feed was choked, whether the liner was fed unevenly, whether tramp metal passed through. A liner that wears evenly to the profile is doing its job; one that shows a deep groove on one side or a hollowed band usually points to a feed or setting problem that a different material will not fix.

## Material baseline: the Mn13 and Mn18 families

Material is the second decision, and for cone liners the industry baseline is high-manganese steel. The grades most commonly specified fall in the Mn13 and Mn18 families, corresponding to the classic austenitic manganese steels covered by ASTM A128. Their behaviour is distinctive: under the repeated impact of a cone chamber, the working surface work-hardens — the outer layer compresses into a skin several times harder than the as-cast metal while the core remains tough — so the same liner resists both the blow and the sliding abrasion that follow it.

| Duty | Grade | Why it is specified |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal ore and aggregate duty | Mn13 | Work-hardens under the chamber's repeated impact |
| Harder feed, large liners that flex under load | Mn18, often as Mn18Cr2 | Higher manganese with a chromium addition for as-cast hardness |
| Fine feed, low impact, sliding abrasion dominant | High-chromium iron, roughly Cr15–Cr26 | Starts hard and holds hardness; needs a machine that tolerates brittleness |

Mn13 suits normal ore and aggregate duty; Mn18, sometimes refined with a chromium addition in the Mn18Cr2 form, is chosen for harder feed and for large liners that flex under load. What matters for the buyer is that the grade is selected against actual working conditions, because the same part number can justify different grades in different pits.

## When chrome beats manganese

Manganese is not the only answer. Where the feed is fine, the impact energy is low, and the wear mechanism is dominated by sliding abrasion rather than impact, a manganese liner may fail to work-harden properly and can wear like a softer steel.

In those conditions the alternative is a high-chromium white iron or an alloy steel with higher as-cast hardness. Chromium-alloy liners in the approximate Cr15 to Cr26 range start hard and hold their hardness, which extends life dramatically in abrasive fines; the trade-off is lower toughness, so they are reserved for applications where the material and the machine can tolerate the brittleness. A liner choice therefore needs to know the feed size, rock type, closed-side setting and the failure pattern of the previous liner — the same information that identifies the part in the first place.

## What the wear pattern tells you

The wear pattern itself is worth reading before it is written off as a material fault.

| Pattern | Likely cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Even wear to the profile | Liner performing to design | Replace on the measured cycle |
| V-shaped groove | Feed segregation or uneven feed spread | Fix the feed, not the material |
| Broken or cracked edge | Oversized feed or tramp metal | Check feed size and tramp protection |
| Cracking around the bolt holes | Liner loose in its seat, or bolts not preloaded correctly | Check seating and bolt preload |

Because these patterns have different causes, the fastest route to longer liner life is usually to send the foundry a photo of the failed part with the running hours — the diagnosis comes back with the replacement, not after it.

## Pattern, tooling and why unit price moves with quantity

The tooling question deserves a direct answer because it is where liner pricing is decided. A cone liner is cast on a pattern or, in the aftermarket, frequently on a pattern cut from a 3D scan of a used liner. The pattern cost is real and it is paid once; it is amortised across the quantity you order, which is why the same liner gets a different unit price at five pieces than at fifty.

When a supplier quotes a liner at a very low price, it is worth asking what the pattern was made from and what the dimensional check against the original part was — because a pattern cut from a worn liner inherits the wear of that liner, and the new casting will come out thinner in the exact zone that already wore out. That single question separates casters who reproduce a worn part from casters who reproduce the drawing.

## Inspection records that ship with the liners

Inspection records complete the liner order. For a cone liner the meaningful evidence is the melt chemistry — the manganese content that confirms the Mn13 or Mn18 grade actually poured — a hardness check, and a dimensional report on the critical faces and bolt-hole pattern.

Large liners with heavy service are sometimes specified with ultrasonic or magnetic-particle testing on the working section, and third-party inspection can be added where the buyer or the end customer requires independent verification. Each item has a cost, so the inspection scope should match the part and the application rather than being applied uniformly; agreeing it in the review means the records ship with the liners instead of being requested after arrival.

## Seating: the failure mode material cannot fix

One more operating point explains a large share of premature liner failures. A cone liner is only as good as its seating: the mantle and the stationary liner are held against machined seats, and a liner that is not fully seated, or that was ordered without the matching set, moves under load, hammers against its seat and cracks from the back regardless of material.

The correct part number with a loose fit fails faster than the wrong part number seated properly. That is why the identification step — dimensions, photos and the machine model — is not administrative paperwork; it is the first line of defence on liner life, and it is free to provide at the start of an inquiry.

## Summary The short version: the mantle moves and the stationary ring may be called either concave or bowl liner, so describe a liner by position, chamber and machine before quoting a part number; Mn13 and Mn18 are the baseline grades and chrome only wins where impact is low; and the wear pattern, not the price list, says whether the last liner was the right one. Buyers who manage liner stocks well treat the cone liner as a system: the mantle and the stationary liner wear at different rates and are rarely changed together, so ordering them in matched sets while keeping one set in stock shortens the change-out window. For a quotation, send: 1. The part number, or the crusher brand and model from the nameplate. 2. The chamber type — coarse, medium or fine. 3. The five measurements in the table above, or photos of the worn liner. 4. The feed size, rock type and closed-side setting. 5. The current liner life in hours, how it failed, the quantity and the delivery market. Tooling, heat treatment and, where specified, machining all sit inside the lead time, so the identity and material decision made today decides the delivery date weeks later. The liners we cast are set out on the cone crusher wear parts page; to send a part for review use the quotation checklist, the contact form, email to hugo@dingdar.com or WhatsApp. The project team confirms identity, chamber profile and material within 12–24 hours and quotes on that confirmed basis.

title: Blow Bars: High Manganese vs High Chrome Steel
excerpt: The material of an impact crusher blow bar decides its life and its price per ton crushed. When manganese work-hardening wins, when high-chrome hardness wins, how bi-metal and ceramic options fit, and the operating conditions that decide the choice.
coverAlt: Foundry worker managing a furnace in an industrial plant
body: **Direct answer:** in an impact crusher, choose the blow bar from the wear mechanism, not from the hardness on paper. If impact wear dominates and the feed can carry oversized rock or tramp metal, high-manganese (Mn13 or Mn18) is the safe answer because it work-hardens under the blow and stays tough. If the feed is clean, well-sized and gritty so sliding abrasion dominates, high-chromium white iron (Cr15–Cr26) can deliver several times the bar life on the same rotor, at the cost of brittleness. Bi-metal and ceramic-insert bars sit between the two: a hard working face on a ductile body, for plants that have outgrown manganese but cannot accept the breakage risk of straight high chrome.

## How an impact crusher loads the bar

In an impact crusher the blow bar is the component that wears fastest, gets changed most often and carries the largest share of the wear cost per ton of product. Every revolution of the rotor sends the bar into the feed, and the bar transfers the kinetic energy that breaks the rock. Because the bar sees the feed at full rotor speed, its material choice has an outsized effect: the difference between a manganese bar and a high-chrome bar on the same rotor can be several times in bar life.

The correct choice is not the one with the higher hardness on paper but the one matched to the impact energy and abrasiveness of the actual feed. Getting that match wrong shows up quickly, in broken bars, in rapid wear, or in a bar that wears slowly but shatters on the first oversized piece.

## Two wear mechanisms act on the same bar

An impact crusher crushes by impact rather than compression. Material enters the rotor path, is struck by the blow bars, is thrown against the stationary impact plates and breaks by the force of the collisions, then falls to the discharge. The blow bar therefore does two mechanical jobs: it imparts the energy and it takes the abrasion of the material passing at rotor speed.

| Mechanism | What causes it | What it demands from the bar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Impact wear | The direct blow of large, heavy feed | Toughness; resistance to cracking and deformation |
| Sliding abrasion | Fine, gritty material scouring the working face | High surface hardness |

The balance between the two is set by the feed: big rocks and low fines produce mostly impact wear; well-crushed, sandy or gritty feed produces mostly abrasive wear. A material choice is really a bet on which mechanism dominates in your application.

## High-manganese steel: the toughness answer

High-manganese steel is the workhorse where impact dominates. The Mn13 and Mn18 grades work-harden under the blow of the rotor: the surface layer compresses into a much harder skin while the interior stays tough, so the bar resists both the impact and a moderate amount of abrasion at the same time.

That combination makes manganese bars the standard recommendation for primary and secondary impact duty with large feed, for concrete and asphalt recycling where the feed carries rebar and other tramp metal, and generally for any application where an oversized piece or a stray piece of steel will find its way into the crusher. The toughness that lets a manganese bar shrug off a piece of rebar is exactly what a high-chrome bar lacks.

The limitation of manganese shows in fine, low-impact feed: without enough impact energy to work-harden the surface, the bar wears comparatively fast and the abrasion advantage belongs to a harder material.

## High-chromium white iron: the abrasion answer

The microstructure of the Cr15 to Cr26 grades contains hard chromium carbides in a supporting matrix, which gives an as-cast hardness far above manganese steel and a resistance to scouring wear that manganese cannot match. In recycling and aggregate applications with clean, well-sized, gritty feed, high-chrome blow bars routinely deliver several times the bar life of manganese on the same rotor, which is the saving that makes the higher price per bar worthwhile.

The same hardness is the weakness: chromium white iron is brittle, and a single oversized boulder or piece of tramp metal that would merely dent a manganese bar can break a high-chrome bar outright. The practical rule is that high chrome earns its cost only where the feed is controlled enough to protect it.

## Bi-metal and composite bars

Between the two families sit the bi-metal and composite bars, which try to keep both advantages. A bi-metal bar is cast with a hard working face, usually a high-chrome alloy, metallurgically bonded to a tough manganese or low-alloy body, so the strike face wears slowly while the mounting end stays ductile enough to take the bending loads of the rotor. A ceramic-insert bar goes further, embedding ceramic tiles in the wear zone for the most abrasive applications.

Both cost more per bar than a single-material bar and pay back only where bar life is the bottleneck and the feed is consistent enough not to break the harder face. They are a middle option for plants that have outgrown manganese but cannot accept the risk of straight high chrome.

## The three families compared

| Family | Typical grades | Strength | Limitation | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| High-manganese steel | Mn13, Mn18 | Work-hardens under impact; very tough; tolerates rebar and tramp metal | Wears fast in fine, low-impact feed | Primary and secondary impact duty with large feed; concrete and asphalt recycling |
| High-chromium white iron | Cr15–Cr26 | Far higher as-cast hardness; resists sliding abrasion; several times bar life on clean gritty feed | Brittle; oversized rock or tramp metal can break it outright | Clean, well-sized, abrasive feed |
| Bi-metal and composite | High-chrome face on manganese or low-alloy body; ceramic inserts | Hard working face with a ductile mounting end | Higher cost per bar; needs consistent feed | Plants that outgrew manganese but cannot risk straight high chrome |

## What the old bar tells you

Wear data separates the decision faster than any brochure:

| Observation | What it suggests | Which way to move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken or cracked bar | Material too brittle for the impact energy, or tramp metal in the feed | Toward toughness, i.e. manganese |
| Smooth, polished wear face | Surface never work-hardened; low impact duty | Toward hardness, i.e. high chrome |
| Uneven wear | Feed distribution or rotor issue, not material | Fix feed spreading or rotor before changing grade |

A foundry that asks for these before quoting is not delaying the quote; it is trying to avoid sending you a bar that repeats the failure.

## The machine is part of the decision

The starting facts are the crusher model and rotor speed, which set the impact energy available; the feed size distribution and abrasiveness, which set the wear mechanism; and the history of the previous bar, its life in hours and how it failed.

Rotor design sets how many bars share the work and how the feed is accelerated: a rotor carrying four bars takes a lighter individual load than one carrying two, which changes how much impact energy each bar absorbs and therefore how far the material choice can lean toward hardness. Rotor speed does the same in a different direction: higher tip speed raises the impact energy delivered to the feed, which favours toughness, while lower speed with the same feed favours a harder, slower-wearing bar.

Two plants crushing the same rock with the same nominal crusher size can legitimately run different bar materials because their rotors run at different speeds. That is why a quote that asks for the machine and the speed is doing the homework that makes the bar last, not delaying the sale.

## Installation and operation

Blow bars are reversible in most rotors: the working edge can be swapped end-for-end or rotated to the opposite face, effectively doubling the life between changes, and the change schedule should track the wear pattern rather than a fixed hour count.

Rotor balance matters: a bar that is heavier than its opposite number vibrates the rotor and shortens bearing life, so bars are weighed and matched on installation. Feed should be spread across the full width of the rotor; a bar fed on one side wears on that side and the imbalance repeats.

Fixing torque is not a detail either: an under-tightened bar moves, pounds its pocket and wears the pocket as well as the bar; an over-tightened bar can distort the mounting seat. The rotor is run in after a change to confirm no vibration before production resumes.

## Cost per ton, not cost per bar

A manganese bar at a lower price that crushes 8,000 tons can be cheaper per ton than a high-chrome bar at double the price that crushes 14,000 tons, or more expensive, depending on the numbers. Plants that record the tons crushed between changes get a simple cost per ton for each material, and that figure settles arguments that no amount of metallurgy talk can.

The same discipline reveals operating faults: a sudden drop in tons per bar is usually a feed, setting or rotor problem appearing before the bar itself is at fault. For stock management, a spare set of bars, matched by weight and balanced, should sit on the shelf before the running set reaches the end of its rotation cycle, because the downtime cost of an unplanned change usually exceeds the bar price several times over.

## Summary and next step

For the buyer, the practical sequence is: confirm the part number or send a photo of the worn bar, state the crusher model and rotor speed, give the feed size and rock type, and record the bar life and failure mode of the current set.

With those details DINGDAR reviews the failure pattern and confirms the material family, manganese, high chrome or a composite, before quoting, so the price reflects the right bar rather than the cheapest one. Send the details through the contact form, by email to hugo@dingdar.com or on WhatsApp, and the technical review comes back within 12–24 hours.
