title: Ball Mill Liners: Materials and What Affects Liner Life
excerpt: Ball mill liners protect the shell and control grinding charge movement. Compare Mn13, Mn18Cr2, high-chrome and rubber liners, then send mill dimensions, media size and current profile for a technical quote.
coverAlt: Worker in protective gear welding metal in an industrial plant
body: **Direct answer:** A ball mill liner is a structural part that wears: the lifter bars lift and release the grinding charge, and the shell plates protect the shell between them, so the profile as much as the material sets grinding efficiency. High-manganese steel is the baseline — Mn13 for standard grinding charges, Mn18Cr2 (nominally 18% manganese with a controlled chromium addition) for larger mills, harder ores and heavier media — while high-chromium iron in the Cr15–Cr26 range takes over where the feed is fine and abrasion dominates impact. Rubber and magnetic liners fit a narrow band of low-impact, downtime-driven applications. The deciding metric is cost per ton ground over full liner life, not price per liner.

## What a mill liner actually does

A ball mill liner is usually treated as a wear part, but it is more accurate to call it a structural part that happens to wear. The liner does two jobs at once: it protects the mill shell from the impact and abrasion of the grinding charge, and its profile controls how that charge is lifted and dropped as the shell rotates. Because the second job decides grinding efficiency, a change of profile or material changes the power draw, the product size and the liner wear together.

The mechanics are simple to picture. The mill shell rotates around a horizontal axis, partially filled with grinding media — steel balls in a ball mill, or the ore plus media in a SAG mill — and the feed to be ground. Rotation speed is normally kept below the critical speed at which the charge would centrifuge; in that window the lifters pick up the charge, carry it partway up the shell and release it, so the media cascade and grind the ore by impact and attrition. Taller lifters raise the charge higher and increase impact energy, flatter profiles let the charge slide and increase abrasion. A liner that has worn its lifters down is, in effect, a different grinding machine than it was when new, which is why monitoring liner height is part of monitoring mill performance and not just maintenance scheduling.

## Lifter bars and shell plates are ordered as a set

Liner design is a family of components rather than a single casting. The common arrangement is a set of lifter bars, which do the lifting, alternating with flat or curved shell plates, which protect the surface between the lifters. The lifter geometry is described by its height, angle and pitch, and mills are often fitted with a wave, step or sinusoidal profile depending on the target.

| Component | Job | What sets its behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifter bars | Lift and release the charge | Height, angle and pitch set the impact energy |
| Shell plates | Protect the shell between the lifters | Profile and thickness set how the charge slides |

The practical consequence for the buyer is that a liner order is a matched set: changing the lifter height without the matching plates, or mixing profiles in one shell, changes the charge behaviour in ways that are hard to predict. That is one more reason the review should see the mill model, the shell dimensions and the current liner profile before a quote.

## Manganese first: Mn13 and Mn18Cr2

High-manganese steel is the baseline for SAG and ball mill liners in the same way it is for crusher wear parts. The Mn13 grade handles the combination of impact and abrasion that a grinding charge produces and work-hardens under the blows of the media.

For larger mills, harder ores and heavier media, the Mn18Cr2 grade — nominally 18% manganese with a controlled chromium addition — is widely specified because the chromium raises the as-cast hardness and improves resistance to the sliding abrasion of the charge while retaining the toughness of the manganese family. Manganese liners are the safe default in the high-energy zones of the mill, near the feed end and wherever large-diameter media are in use.

## Chrome, rubber and magnetic: where each fits

Chromium-alloy liners — the high-chromium white irons in roughly the Cr15 to Cr26 range — take over where the wear mechanism shifts toward abrasion. In a mill grinding fine, highly abrasive feed with relatively small media and lower impact energy, a chrome liner starts hard and stays hard, and its life can exceed manganese by a wide margin. The restriction is the same as in any chrome wear part: brittleness. A mill running large balls, or a shell whose worn profile lets the liner flex, can crack a chrome liner, and a cracked liner fails as a protection barrier as well as a wear surface.

Beyond steel, rubber and composite liners are a serious option for a specific band of applications. Rubber is lighter than steel, cheaper to handle and change, and dampens noise and the impact of smaller media; it is widely used in secondary grinding of abrasive ores where impact energy is modest. The limits are temperature, media size and sharp, coarse feed that can tear the rubber. Magnetic liners, built around permanent magnets, hold a layer of grinding media and fines against the shell and use that layer as the wearing surface — an established option in fine-grinding mills where downtime is the dominant cost.

| Liner family | Where it fits | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mn13 | Standard grinding charge, high-energy zones near the feed end | Tough and work-hardening; less resistance where abrasion dominates |
| Mn18Cr2 | Larger mills, harder ores, heavier media | Higher as-cast hardness and abrasion resistance, keeps manganese toughness |
| High-chromium iron, Cr15–Cr26 | Fine abrasive feed, small media, low impact energy | Starts hard and stays hard; brittle under large balls or a flexing shell |
| Rubber and composite | Secondary grinding of abrasive ores, modest impact | Lighter, quieter, easier to change; limited by temperature and media size |
| Magnetic | Fine-grinding mills where downtime is the dominant cost | Uses a held media layer as the wear surface; a specific fit, not a default |

The material question is not "which is best" but "which fits this mill, this media and this feed", and it is answered with the same operating data as the profile question. The boundary between manganese and chrome is set by impact energy and liner loading, not by price.

## What decides liner life

Most of the factors that decide liner life are on the operator side of the ledger.

| Variable | What it sets | Where it is controlled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Media size and charge volume | Impact energy delivered to the liner | Charge management |
| Feed size, hardness and abrasiveness | Wear rate of the working surface | Feed control and blending |
| Mill speed and pulp level | How the charge behaves | Operating setpoints |
| Liner profile wearing over time | Lift, and therefore all of the above | Change-out planning on measured thickness |

In practice, two identical liners in two mills rarely give the same life, and the difference is usually traceable to these variables rather than to the casting. Liner life is normally tracked by measuring residual thickness or lifter height at agreed points during scheduled stops; the trend tells you when the change-out is due before the liner fails, which protects the shell from damage and keeps the charge profile stable to the end of life.

## Installation: more liners fail at fitting than in service

A mill liner set is fitted against machined shell seats and held by bolts that pass through the shell; the preload on those bolts is what keeps the liner from moving when the charge lands on it, and an under-torqued liner hammers its seat and cracks, exactly like a loose cone liner.

Fitting also means matching the lifter and plate sequence of the design: mixing profiles in one shell, or leaving a worn lifter in place beside new ones, changes the charge lift and produces wear that looks like a material fault. Practical mills schedule the change with a full inspection of the shell and the bolt condition, and they keep the records of which profile and grade were fitted where — the history that makes the next material recommendation a calculation rather than a guess.

## Cost per ton ground, not price per liner

The cost picture keeps liner selection honest. The liner is part of the grinding cost, and the cheapest liner is not always the cheapest grinding: a profile that loses its lift early drops grinding efficiency, so the mill draws power to produce less work while the liner still has thickness left. Conversely, a longer-life material that is mismatched to the feed can crack or distort and stop the mill on an unplanned basis, which is far more expensive than a planned change.

The decision metric that matters is cost per ton ground over the full liner life, including planned and unplanned downtime — not the price per liner. Plants that track power draw per ton alongside liner life see the trade-off clearly, and that is the same data a foundry needs to confirm the next grade.

## Inspection records for a mill liner order

Inspection evidence closes the loop on a mill liner order in the same way it does on crusher parts. The records that matter are the melt chemistry confirming the grade actually poured — the manganese and chromium content for Mn18Cr2, or the chromium range for a chrome liner — a hardness verification, and a dimensional report on the lifter heights and the shell contact faces.

Large mill liners in heavy service can justify ultrasonic or magnetic-particle testing on the working section, and third-party inspection is available where the project demands it. The scope is agreed in the review so the records travel with the shipment; a buyer who specifies the evidence before production receives it with the liners, instead of waiting for it after arrival. And because the quote is built on a confirmed profile, material and inspection scope, the price and delivery date in the quotation are the ones the order follows.

## Summary The short version: a mill liner is a matched set of lifters and shell plates, its profile decides grinding efficiency as much as its material does, Mn13 covers standard charges while Mn18Cr2 handles larger mills and heavier media, and chrome only pays where impact is low and abrasion dominates. Judge it on cost per ton ground, and settle the grade with measured lifter height at change-out rather than with a price comparison. When the next liner change is being planned, the information that produces a useful quote is: 1. The mill model, shell diameter and length. 2. The media size and charge. 3. The feed type and size. 4. The current liner profile and life in hours. 5. The residual thickness measured at change-out. 6. The inspection scope required, and the delivery market. DINGDAR reviews the profile and material together — Mn13, Mn18Cr2, chrome or a composite — and confirms the inspection scope before quoting, with technical feedback within 12–24 hours of receiving the details. The specific parts we cast — shell liners, lifter bars, head and end liners and grate plates — are set out on ball mill liners, which also lists the six records to send with a liner enquiry; the contact routes are the quotation checklist, the contact form, email to hugo@dingdar.com or WhatsApp.

title: Mn13 Jaw Plates: Grades, Work Hardening & Specification
excerpt: What "Mn13" actually means on a jaw plate, how work hardening gives it long life in crushing, when Mn18 or an alloy grade is the better call, and the information that turns a part number into a reliable quotation.
coverAlt: Foundry worker inspecting castings on a production floor
body: **Direct answer:** Mn13 jaw plates are cast austenitic manganese steel (nominally ~13% Mn, in the ASTM A128 family), not cut plate. As cast they sit near 200 HB and stay tough; under impact the working face work-hardens into roughly 450–550 HBW while the core stays austenitic. Mn13 suits standard quarry and aggregate feed. Mn18, Mn18Cr2 or Mn22 are specified for harder feed and for larger plates that flex under load, and an alloy or higher-chromium grade is the better start when the feed is fine and low-impact and the surface never hardens.

## What Mn13 actually contains

Mn13 jaw plates are the default wear material for the fixed and movable jaws of jaw crushers, and the name carries real information: a manganese content around 13 percent in the Hadfield family of austenitic manganese steels, the same material family covered by ASTM A128. Mn13 is a family, not a single recipe. The nominal 13% manganese sits in a specification band, and the same family extends upward for heavier duty:

| Grade | Manganese | Carbon | Chromium | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mn13 | ~11.5–14% | ~1.1–1.35% | — | Standard jaw plate duty |
| Mn13Cr2 | ~11.5–14% | ~1.1–1.35% | ~1.7–2.2% | Higher as-cast hardness, better sliding abrasion |
| Mn18 | ~17–19% | — | — | Heavier duty |
| Mn18Cr2 | ~17–19% | — | Chromium-bearing | Harder feed, large plates |
| Mn22 | ~21–23% | — | Chromium-bearing | Very heavy, high-impact duty |

Silicon sits around 0.3–1.0%, with sulphur and phosphorus held low. The chromium in the Mn13Cr2 form raises the as-cast hardness and improves resistance to sliding abrasion without giving up the toughness of the manganese family.

Ranges like these are published by most foundries, but they are typical bands, not a guarantee. The meaningful number is the melt chemistry of the actual heat, confirmed by a material certificate against the standard agreed for the order, an ASTM A128-series or GB equivalent.

## Why it hardens where it is hit

As cast, and after the water-quench treatment that gives it a full austenitic structure, the plate is comparatively soft, which makes it ductile and tough enough to absorb the shock of a boulder landing on the jaw. Under repeated impact, the surface layer deforms and transforms: the austenite in the working face converts to a much harder martensite, while the core stays austenitic and tough.

| Condition | Typical hardness | What it means in service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As cast, after water quench | Around 200 HB | Ductile and tough; absorbs impact without cracking |
| Work-hardened surface layer | Roughly 450–550 HBW | Martensitic skin resists wear |
| Core | Stays austenitic | Retains the toughness reserve |

The plate effectively wears in a hardened skin and rests on a tough body, which is why a correctly loaded Mn13 jaw plate can outlast a harder-looking steel that starts hard but has no reserve of toughness. The same mechanism explains the limitation: without impact, the surface does not harden, and Mn13 in a low-impact, fine-feed duty can wear like a softer steel.

## A jaw plate is a casting, not a cut piece

One distinction matters when buyers compare prices: a jaw plate is a casting, not a cut piece of plate. Mn13 steel is also supplied as rolled plate for liners and chutes, but crusher jaws are cast to the part geometry, tooth profile, mounting holes and all, through green sand, shell moulding or lost foam, depending on size and complexity.

A plate that is simply cut or machined from rolled Mn13 stock lacks the cast tooth geometry that makes the jaw bite, and its through-thickness properties are not the same as a casting poured for the part. The price comparison that matters is between castings of the same grade and review scope, not between a casting and a piece of stock steel. Ask what the plate was cast from and how it was made, not only what grade is stamped on it.

## Mn13, Mn18Cr2 or Mn22: which duty needs which grade

Within the manganese family, the choice follows the loading:

| Duty | Typical grade | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard quarry and aggregate feed (granite, basalt, limestone), plates rigid enough to pass impact into the surface | Mn13 | Work-hardens under normal impact |
| Harder feed, larger plates that flex under load | Mn18, especially Mn18Cr2 | Higher as-cast hardness and better surface resistance, with a tough core |
| Very heavy, high-impact duty, large plates, very hard rock | Mn22 | Highest manganese content, usually with chromium |
| Fine, low-impact feed where the surface polishes instead of hardening | Alloy steel or a higher-chromium option | Needs initial hardness rather than work hardening |

The same part number can justify different grades in different pits, which is why a foundry that quotes a grade before asking about the feed is quoting on hope, not on data.

## What the failure pattern tells you

Failure patterns decide whether the grade was right:

- **Cracks through the plate.** Usually oversized feed, tramp metal, or a plate that was not fully seated. A different grade will not cure it.
- **Smooth, polished wear face in fine low-impact feed.** The surface never hardened; an alloy steel or a higher-chromium option with more initial hardness can last longer.
- **Uneven wear, one corner or one side fast.** Feed distribution or jaw setting, not material.

Photographs of the worn plate with the running hours attached are the fastest diagnostic a foundry receives, and they are worth more than a verbal description of the failure.

## Machine coverage

Jaw plates are produced to reference across the common jaw crusher ranges, the C-series and LT-class machines, the J and JM classes, Kue Ken and Terex Pegson machines, and the many PE and PEX models used across Asia and Latin America, as well as to drawing, 3D model or sample.

The part number cast on the back of the plate is the fastest reference; where it has worn away, a tape measure on the tooth profile and bolt pattern plus a photo of the mounting face is enough to match. Produced to reference means the geometry, bolt holes and tooth form are reproduced to the original part, with the grade and inspection scope confirmed in review. The machine name is the starting point, not the whole specification.

## What to send for a quotation For a reliable quotation, the foundry needs: 1. The crusher model and part number, or a photo of the worn plate. 2. The typical feed size and rock type. 3. The closed-side setting. 4. The current plate life in hours, and how the old plate failed. 5. The quantity and delivery market. With those facts DINGDAR confirms the grade, hardness and inspection scope before quoting, and replies with technical feedback within 12–24 hours. The fixed and movable jaw plates we cast, and the review process behind them, are laid out on the jaw crusher wear parts page; the material selection logic for the manganese family is covered in our guide to choosing jaw plate material.

## Installation decides how much life you actually get

A jaw plate is clamped against the frame by wedges or bolts, and the fixing must hold the plate tight against its seat: a loose plate hammers, cracks from the back and wears its seat, regardless of grade.

Mn13 plates are generally fitted as cast or with light grinding on the mounting face. The jaw setting interacts with the plate profile: a worn tooth profile changes the crushing angle and the product shape long before the plate is thin. Checking the seat, the wedges and the setting at each change is cheap maintenance that shows up directly in plate life.

## The certificate is what proves the grade

For Mn13 the meaningful evidence is the melt or heat analysis, which states the manganese, carbon and chromium actually poured against the agreed standard; a hardness figure on the as-cast or treated state; and a dimensional report on the tooth profile and the mounting face, because a plate that does not seat does not last.

Buyers who order Mn13 without specifying the standard or the records receive plates labelled Mn13. The certificate is what turns the label into a verifiable fact. Inspection scope is agreed in the review, so the records travel with the shipment rather than being requested after arrival.

## Cost per ton, not cost per plate

Mn13 costs more than a plain carbon or low-alloy casting at the same weight, and it pays for itself only through longer life, which depends on the duty actually hardening the surface.

A plant that records tons crushed per set, and the failure mode at change-out, gets a simple cost per ton that settles the grade question faster than any brochure. Two plants crushing the same rock can legitimately see different economics for the same plate grade because their settings, feed and maintenance differ. That is why the data from your own plant is the deciding input, not a generic claim about life.

## Summary The short version: Mn13 jaw plates are cast, not cut; they harden where they are hit; Mn13 covers standard duty while Mn18 and alloy grades step in for harder feed; and a photo of the worn plate plus the machine reference beats a drawing request every time. To start a review, send the part number, a photo of the worn plate, or the crusher model through the contact form, by email to hugo@dingdar.com, or on WhatsApp. The technical review confirms the grade and inspection scope within 12–24 hours, and the quotation is built on the confirmed facts.

title: How to Choose Ball Mill Liners: Mn13, Mn18Cr2, High Chrome or Rubber?
excerpt: A practical ball mill liner selection guide: compare Mn13, Mn18Cr2, high-chrome and rubber liners by impact, abrasion, mill zone and inspection needs before requesting a quote.
coverAlt: Foundry worker inspecting castings on a production floor
metaDescription: How to choose ball mill liners: compare Mn13, Mn18Cr2, high-chrome and rubber by mill zone, impact, abrasion, media size and inspection needs before a quote.
body:
## Direct answer: choose the liner from the duty, not from the material name

The right ball mill liner matches four operating facts: **mill zone, grinding-media impact, feed abrasiveness and liner profile**. Mn13 or Mn18Cr2 manganese steel is usually the starting point for high-impact shell, head and end-liner duty. Pearlitic chrome-moly steel or high-chromium cast iron becomes more relevant when sliding abrasion dominates and impact energy is controlled. Rubber or composite systems can be considered where lower weight, noise reduction or easier handling matters and the feed and temperature are compatible.

A material label alone is not enough. The same mill can need different materials at the feed end, shell and discharge end, and the selection can change as feed size, media size, throughput or liner profile changes.

## What do ball mill liners do?

Ball mill liners perform two jobs: they protect the mill shell and heads from repeated impact and abrasive contact, and they control charge movement through lifter height, face angle, pitch and shell coverage. Shell liners work with lifter bars to lift and release the grinding media. Head and end liners protect the feed and discharge ends, where impact direction and slurry movement differ from the cylindrical shell. Grate plates in grate-discharge mills also influence pulp flow and retention.

This is why liner selection is not only a wear-resistance decision. A profile that lifts the charge too aggressively can increase impact and power demand; a profile that has worn too far can reduce the intended grinding action even when metal remains on the shell.

## Step 1: identify the liner position and mill duty

Start by separating the order into shell liners and lifter bars, feed-end or head liners, discharge-end liners, and grate plates or pulp-lifter components where applicable. Then record the mill type and operating duty. A ball mill, rod mill, regrind mill and SAG-related application do not impose the same loading pattern. Rod mills generally use a more rolling charge and need a profile that avoids damaging or tangling the rods. Ball mills use a media charge whose size, volume and impact energy influence both profile and material selection.

Do not mix a new lifter profile with an old shell-plate arrangement without reviewing the complete set. Lifter height, angle and spacing work as a system; changing one element can change charge motion and the wear pattern of the others.

## Step 2: separate impact wear from sliding abrasion

| Observed condition | Likely selection direction | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Large media, coarse feed, repeated impact or deformation | Mn13 or Mn18Cr2 manganese steel | Media diameter, charge volume, feed size and liner support |
| Smooth, progressive abrasion with controlled impact | Pearlitic chrome-moly or high-chrome alloy | Ore abrasiveness, mill speed, temperature and crack history |
| Lower-impact secondary grinding where handling weight matters | Rubber or composite option, if compatible | Media size, feed sharpness, temperature and fixing method |
| Cracking, loose bolts or broken sections | Review installation and loading before changing grade | Bolt preload, shell seat, tramp material and liner fit |
| Uneven end-only or one-sided wear | Review feed distribution and operating conditions | Pulp level, feed entry, mill alignment and charge distribution |

A harder grade is not automatically better. High-chromium iron can offer strong abrasion resistance, but it has less tolerance for heavy impact and tramp material than a tough manganese grade. Manganese may wear inefficiently if the application does not provide enough impact for work hardening.

## Step 3: compare the main ball mill liner materials

### Mn13 manganese steel

Mn13 is a common starting point for high-impact grinding duty. Its value is the combination of toughness and work hardening: the working surface can become harder under repeated impact while the core retains toughness. It is commonly considered for shell, head and end-liner applications where the charge is heavy or the feed is coarse. If the feed is fine and impact energy is low, the surface may not work harden as expected.

### Mn18Cr2 manganese steel

Mn18Cr2 is considered when the application needs a manganese-family liner with higher initial hardness and strong impact tolerance. It can be relevant for larger mills, heavier media or harder feed, but the exact grade and heat-treatment requirements should be confirmed against the project specification and material certificate.

### Pearlitic chrome-moly steel

Pearlitic chrome-moly steel is a low-alloy, heat-treated option used where wear is more abrasive and impact is moderate. It can hold a liner profile predictably and is often considered for rod-mill and ball-mill applications with controlled impact. Confirm the hardness range, section thickness, heat treatment, mill zone and history of cracking or breakage.

### High-chromium cast iron

High-chromium cast iron is designed for high abrasion resistance. ASTM A532 is a relevant standard reference for abrasion-resistant cast irons used in mining, milling and earth-handling applications. High-chrome liners are most defensible where abrasion dominates and impact is controlled; they need caution with large balls, coarse feed, tramp material or high liner flexing.

### Rubber and composite systems

Rubber and composite liners can be appropriate in selected secondary or fine-grinding duties. Possible advantages include lower handling weight, noise reduction and easier relining. Limits depend on media size, temperature, feed sharpness, chemical conditions and the fixing system. Compare them with steel on full operating cost, including liner life, relining time, handling equipment and downtime.

## Step 4: inspect the worn liner before changing the material

Record residual thickness at agreed shell and head positions, lifter height and face-angle change, cracks or deformation, wear concentration near feed or discharge, current liner life in hours and tonnes milled, media size and charge volume, feed material and size, and any recent process changes.

If wear accelerated after a change in feed size, media size, throughput or mill speed, changing the alloy without correcting the condition may only hide the root cause. Photographs of the working face and mounting face are especially useful when a drawing is unavailable.

## Step 5: confirm profile, fit and inspection scope

A liner set should be reviewed as matched geometry. Confirm the mill model, shell diameter and length, bolt pattern, liner section thickness, lifter arrangement, grate details and machining or fit requirements.

For a B2B order, define the inspection package before production. Depending on the application, this may include melt chemistry or a material certificate, heat-treatment record, hardness verification, dimensional report, visual inspection, non-destructive testing where justified and third-party inspection where required. DINGDAR reviews shell liners, lifter bars, head and end liners and grate plates against a drawing, sample, worn part or reference through the [Ball Mill Liners](https://dingdar.com/ball-mill-liners/) page and technical contact process.

## What should buyers send for a ball mill liner quotation?

A quote-ready information pack includes the mill model, shell diameter and length, liner position, current drawing or OEM part number, clear worn-liner photographs, media diameter and charge volume, feed material and size, current liner material and profile, service life, residual-thickness measurements if available, required quantity, delivery market and inspection documents. If a drawing is unavailable, a part number, machine model and clear photographs can still start the technical review.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best material for ball mill liners?

There is no single best material for every mill. Mn13 or Mn18Cr2 is generally considered for high-impact duty; pearlitic chrome-moly and high-chrome materials are considered when abrasion dominates and impact is controlled; rubber or composite options may suit selected lower-impact applications.

### What are shell liners in a ball mill?

Shell liners protect the cylindrical mill shell and work with lifter bars to control how the grinding charge is lifted and released. Their profile affects charge movement, grinding action and wear distribution.

### Are ball mill shell liners and head liners the same?

No. Shell liners protect the cylindrical barrel, while head or end liners protect the feed and discharge ends. They experience different loading and are normally specified as separate components within a matched liner set.

### When should a mill use Mn18Cr2 instead of Mn13?

Mn18Cr2 may be considered when the mill has heavier media, harder feed, larger sections or a duty requiring higher initial hardness while retaining manganese-family toughness. The decision should be checked against the current wear pattern, media size and crack history.

### When are high-chrome liners suitable?

High-chrome liners are most suitable when abrasive wear dominates and impact is controlled. They need caution in coarse-feed, large-media or tramp-material conditions because crack resistance may be more important than maximum hardness.

### How can liner life be measured correctly?

Track operating hours and tonnes milled together with residual thickness or lifter height at agreed measurement points. Also record feed, media, throughput and mill-speed changes so comparisons reflect the operating condition.

### Can ball mill liners be produced to a drawing or OEM part number?

Yes. A drawing, OEM reference, machine model or worn sample can be used to review geometry. The material, hardness, fit, inspection scope and quotation basis should be confirmed in writing before production.

## Conclusion

Choose ball mill liners by matching **profile, position, impact energy, abrasion, media and operating history**. Mn13 and Mn18Cr2 are practical starting points for high-impact manganese duty; chrome-moly and high-chrome materials become more relevant as controlled abrasion increases; rubber and composite solutions belong to a narrower, application-specific range. The most useful comparison is cost per ton ground over the full liner life, including relining time and unplanned downtime.

Further reading: [DINGDAR Ball Mill Liners](https://dingdar.com/ball-mill-liners/), [DINGDAR Ball Mill Liners: Materials and What Affects Liner Life](https://dingdar.com/news/ball-mill-liners-mn18cr2-guide/), [Bradken Mill Liner Solutions](https://www.bradken.com/blogs/why-choose-bradkens-mill-liner-solutions), [FLSmidth Mill Liners](https://www.flsmidth.com/en/products/mill-liners), and [ASTM A532/A532M Standard Specification for Abrasion-Resistant Cast Irons](https://webstore.ansi.org/standards/astm/astma532a532m93a1999e1?srsltid=AYCX9vJG9Igor7YKfKoyM41_YoBte47a_PFmj8LdexlpbrQByFwEx3K5a).
